We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that integrates object points with their relative positions in relation to a robot. Our approach achieves superior performance in pose estimation and close-to-state-of-the-art results in object manipulation. In the study of magnetism and electronic properties, the unique orbital arrangements in transition metal ions play a significant role. It is particularly narrow for compounds featuring direct interactions between transition metals with different shell fillings, as seen in the ferromagnetic interaction between manganese (3d electrons) and cobalt (4d electrons) in MnCo2S4 compounds.  A recent example of such a direct interaction has been observed between copper (3d electrons) and iron (3d electrons) in cupricite, leading to unusual consequences where all the orbital levels are filled except for a lone band that shows an anomalous broadening that cannot be accounted for by known mechanisms.  A theoretical analysis using a combination of band calculations and many-body approaches provides an in-depth understanding of the unique orbital behavior observed in cupricite. It is also observed that applying pressure or magnetic fields alters the anomalous broadening of the orbital levels or even fills the last orbital level in these compounds.  The study of these effects is considered worthwhile as they could lead to novel quantum states and orbital-filled ferromagnetism. A novel, previously unreported phenomenon called "dark-state Rabi oscillations" has been observed in a specific type of exciton called "F-center excitons," which are formed within aluminum oxide layers, often encountered as barriers in quantum heterostructures. These oscillations between a localized F-center exciton and a mobile electron in a nearby donor atom occur in the absence of an external magnetic field, are influenced by the spatial arrangement of the involved particles, and can result in the formation of localized and mobile populations that repeatedly switch between their initial and final states over time. This phenomenon has been extensively examined through a combination of theoretical modeling, incorporating various levels of complexity, and direct comparison with experimental findings, and its distinctive features enable it to be identified in future experiments. This discovery is particularly significant because it converts a complex, often unpredictable many-body process called "light-matter interaction" into a highly regular, predictable motion, demonstrates the potential for constructing robust and controllable dark states within planar, two-dimensional materials, and offers a novel means of investigating and exploiting excited states called "J-aggregates" and "mott insulators" that rely on the spatial arrangement of their constituent particles. This finding also highlights the capabilities of a specific experimental setup called "micro-photoluminescence" that enables both precise control over light-matter interaction and simultaneous examination of its effects. This achievement is also a result of collaboration between experimental and theoretical solid-state physics groups, who worked together to uncover the underlying causes of this phenomenon and validate their findings with a combination of theoretical modeling, experimental modification, and direct comparison with related phenomena. This discovery is anticipated to lead to a better comprehension of complex light-matter interactions, which are a prequisite for creating future quantum technologies, and to provide novel insights into the unique properties of F-center excitons, that could potentially be harnessed to develop new applications for aluminum oxide layers. This achievement could also pave the way for exploring and manipulating other excited states that rely on the spatial arrangement of their constituent particles, and could lead to a better comprehension of phenomena such as "Anderson localization" and "Bose-Einstein condensates." We introduce a technique for creating polynomial functions in an LP-based reinforcement learning framework, which originates from a linear regression model. Unlike other methods that use piecewise representations with explicit state divisions, our approach uses an integer programming problem to determine state divisions based on polynomial coefficients. This results in a compact representation with typically fewer divisions than alternative methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique on a cart-pole swing up task and a real-world application involving a gas turbine, showing that it outperforms other methods in terms of representation size while achieving comparable performance. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghulkin/polymath.

A novel framework called DDAUnet for comprehensively identifying neoplasms in the esophagus from CT scans has been proposed. This model combines advanced techniques such as dense attention and dense UNet to create an efficient and precise method for producing an initial set of potential neoplastic regions. A second stage of the model involving spatial attention and UNet enhances the precision of these regions by conducting an in-depth analysis of the CT data. Experimental results showed this approach outperformed existing benchmarks in both initial region detection and precise segmentation tasks. Furthermore, DDAUnet demonstrated significant advantages in terms of computation efficiency compared to the current state-of-the-art models. Evaluations conducted on real-world data also supported the potential applications of this method in developing automatic neoplasm detection systems for clinical use. Such systems could greatly assist specialists in identifying neoplastic regions more quickly and accurately. The proliferation of image descriptions has been recently substantial, due in part to artificial intelligence's ability to generate them, and has various practical applications. Despite the benefits, there is still a need to evaluate the accuracy of these descriptions. Current assessment metrics rely on complex mathematical theories that require human references, but these references are time-consuming and costly to obtain. This paper explores alternative approaches to using reference information, including utilizing a single expert's descriptions or no descriptions at all. We evaluate and compare these approaches using real-world references and demonstrate simple, more practical assessment methods. Additionally, we provide a freely available online tool for experimenting with these approaches. The data and software associated with this research are accessible at https://github.com/ghritli/HD. Previous studies attributed varying levels of significance to the Big Geographic Sort, an observable pattern where large groups of Americans with similar socioeconomic characteristics tend to reside in specific geographical areas. Our analysis focuses on 100 major U.S. cities while utilizing socioeconomic data from Reddit users. We discovered that the Big Geographic Sort is indeed a factor, influencing how misinformation spreads within each city. It appears that users from high-density, economically affluent areas tend to distrust information easily, whereas users from low-density, less affluent areas are more open to accepting information. Notably, the relationship between the Big Geographic Sort and misinformation dissemination varies across cities. It is essential to consider the distinct social and economic characteristics of each location when developing strategies to combat the spread of misinformation. Furthermore, additional research is necessary to understand the underlying causes of the Big Geographic Sort and its implications for information dissemination. The findings presented in this study can be applied to other domains, such as vaccine hesitancy and political polarization. The associated dataset is available for public use. The discoveries reported in this study are novel, offering a unique perspective on the Big Geographic Sort and providing a novel explanation for the uneven distribution of misinformation. Humans naturally pick up on instructions that include auditory guidance, which enables efficient learning and performance for new activities. As robots are set to work alongside people, being able to effectively comprehend audio instructions will be crucial. Presently, research on audio instruction comprehension has focused mainly on spoken language, without much consideration of its underlying acoustic properties. This study delves into the underlying patterns of spoken instructions, focusing on how they are structurally and statistically organized. An advanced neural network, specifically a Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) and Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN), was utilized to extract key acoustic features from a substantial dataset of human instructions. The analysis revealed that task-dependent elements, such as instructions related to grasping and releasing, share similar acoustic characteristics. Furthermore, an intuitive visualization was created to demonstrate the complex patterns of the dataset, showcasing how GCNN effectively learned the underlying representations of the data. This study's findings contribute to the advancement of research on audio instruction comprehension, while the developed model also provides a valuable tool for analyzing large datasets of spoken language. This technology has been applied in a related project called "Listen to Learn," which is designed to train robots using auditory feedback for enhanced performance. This study's approach can be tailored to suit a variety of tasks and datasets, offering a versatile solution with wide-ranging potential applications. We illustrate how Euler-Arnold equations, a broader differential equation category, can be applied to conformal field theory, resulting in its intricate form. Specifically, we derive the exact relationship between these equations and conformal field theory, providing detailed examples such as linear sigma models and their applications in physics. Furthermore, our approach enables us with the capacity to address high-order correlation functions effortlessly. Additionally, we offer a new, intricate form of the Ward anomaly equation, which is essential for automatically obtaining correlation functions from conformal field theory. This new equation, combined with Euler-Arnold equations and Euler-Arnold transport equations, forms a comprehensive set of differential equations that can be used to solve correlation functions. This approach is particularly relevant for evaluating correlation functions in linear sigma models. This framework also provides a new perspective on the properties of conformal field theory itself. Creating conversational agents that engage in natural-language conversations with humans has become a highly sought-after goal in recent years. While significant progress has been made, there are still many challenges to overcome in achieving this objective. Most current approaches rely on human evaluation, which can be time-consuming, expensive, and subject to personal biases. A promising alternative is a automated testing framework that leverages a controller similar to those found in reinforcement learning, enabling the systematic validation of bots through a series of inputs and output assessments. This paper introduces a novel automated testing platform for conversational agents, incorporating a range of validation techniques that can be used individually or in combination to ensure the reliability and accuracy of bots. It also explores the possibility of using automated validation as a substitute for human assessment, examining various comparison metrics that gauge the similarity between human and automated evaluations. The testing system, along with the evaluation studies, are made available online to facilitate further development and validation. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/AmrUmair/METRIS-CFB. The evaluation datasets can be found at https://github.com/AmrUmair/METRIS-CFB-datasets. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Most existing methods focus on integrating information across domains, but do not effectively address the issue of heterogeneity in source and target domains. Current approaches often rely on the assumption that domains can be homogeneous, but real-world scenarios defy this assumption. In response to this challenge, a new cross-domain recommendation framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation via Enhanced Comprehensive Attribute Preference Learning (MSDCAPL) is proposed. This approach leverages a rich representation of user attributes and item items to address both data sparsity and domain heterogeneity. The proposed framework utilizes a unique multi-task learning design, combining the strengths of attribute-based and collaborative learning, to effectively manage domain heterogeneity. Furthermore, HDC is employed to derive a dense and compact representation of user attributes and items, while the use of Gaussian Mixture Model-based outlier robust regression ensures resistance to noise and outlier user or item data. The effectiveness of MSDCAPL is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets, highlighting its superior performance in addressing data sparsity and domain heterogeneity. The proposed approach offers a powerful and scalable tool for managing noise and outliers, while facilitating applications in various scenarios, including but not limited to cross-domain recommendation. The code for MSDCAPL is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhoukai1997/MSDCAPL.

In a setting with competing agents, we examine a meeting scenario where decision-making occurs behind closed doors. Within the meeting, agents can collaborate, but outside the meeting, their actions are driven by individual interests. We develop a model incorporating multiple meetings and incentive systems. As meetings are often recurring, accounting for past conversations and establishing policies to adapt to changing situations is crucial. Our focus is on a simple model featuring two agents in one meeting, with each agent pursuing a separate goal. We show that the model yields meaningful results, including the emergence of dominant equilibrium policies and the effectiveness of meetings in driving meaningful change outside the meeting context. To expand the model, we introduce constraints and multiple meetings, while maintaining analytical solutions for key performance indicators. Next, we develop an approximate value-function approach for more complex scenarios, including large numbers of meetings, varying session lengths, and intricate outside-world dynamics. This leads to a system with appealing properties, allowing us to harness the advantages of policy improvement and policy execution. We validate this approach through challenging simulated environments. Lastly, we explore a pure exploration strategy in a setting with uncertain outside-world dynamics, demonstrating its ability to adapt to both beneficial and harmful actions discovered during the meeting. In this process, we illustrate the statistical significance of our findings across multiple independent simulations. The paper contributes a novel drive-based incentive meeting model, along with multiple applications showcasing its value in specific contexts. These scenarios include competing agents in one meeting, with varying levels of session length, outside-world dynamics, and constraints, as well as multimeeting setups and pure exploration scenarios. The corresponding code is available at https://github.com/Shouran/Incentive-Meeting.

This paper introduces a novel structure called T hubs, which are composed of T-type directional couplers and are implemented in a silicon-on-insulator material. We have theoretically proven that T hubs are capable of effectively achieving the function of a 2x2 multimode interferometer, while also being highly resistant to cross-talk and backlash. Utilizing a finite-difference time-domain simulator, we have found that T hubs can maintain their functionality even after withstanding a high level of focal intensity. Additionally, our calculations indicate that T hubs can be designed to operate within a specific wavelength range, which can be achieved by creating a spatial reservoir in the T-type directional couplers through etching. We have also explored the possibility of etching a MMI, and have discovered that it can be converted into a bismuth rib type, while maintaining high coupling rates and low backscatter. A 50x50 $\mu$m2 silicon-on-insulator T hub has been successfully fabricated and tested, which shows that it has a low backscatter level of 0.0004, a high coupling rate of 98.8%, and the ability to operate within a specific wavelength range. Our experimental findings have been verified through measurements, and we believe that this novel T hub design has vast potential applications in the fields of quantum computing, biophotonic imaging, and nonlinear optics. A corresponding device, made from silicon-on-insulator material, with a 50x50 $\mu$m2 footprint, has also been proposed and analyzed. A 100x100 $\mu$m2 silicon-on-insulator T hub has been proposed and analyzed, which exhibits unique resonant properties and allows for the generation of a narrow spectral line due to four-wave mixing, while also allowing for the conversion of a 1550 nm signal to a 630 nm signal with an conversion rate of 20%. Given a closed, symplectic $n$-manifold carrying $k$ independent Hamiltonian torus actions with compact groups $G_1,\ldots,G_k$, this paper provides a criterion for which $H$-actions are admissible, where $H$ is a compact connected Lie group with rank less than $k$. Specifically, we find that an $H$-action is acceptable if, for any $i$ in the range $1 \dots k$, it holds that the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}_i$ contains the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}$, which implies that the corresponding moment maps satisfy a specific alteration property, thereby yielding a specific symmetry. Additionally, we establish that this criterion is necessary, albeit a more elementary proof is offered for a particular instance. Moreover, another interpretation of this criterion is provided, showing that it is equivalent to the action being Hamiltonian under a particular alteration of its associated moment map, which in turn is equivalent to the action being Hamiltonian in a different, symplectic context. Finally, we offer some examples and a more general development called the alteration theorem.

Recent studies using word embedding models for sentiment analysis have relied heavily on the Loughran-McDonald corpus, which is a widely used set of press releases with emotionally charged language. Many have interpreted the effectiveness of these models in this context as evidence of their ability to grasp semantic meaning. However, a closer examination is needed to determine if these models are truly capturing the intended meaning, particularly with regards to word embeddings that represent positive and negative sentiment. To address this, a more in-depth analysis of these models is conducted, taking into account the complex relationships between words and their context. A novel approach is presented that combines supervised learning with unsupervised methods to better assess the ability of these models to capture the semantic meaning of words. The evaluation framework developed in this research includes both quantitative and qualitative components to examine the representations generated by these models. The results show that the representations are largely determined by the learning algorithm used, rather than any inherent semantic properties, and that they fail to account for the distinct categories of words, such as proper nouns and abbreviations. Furthermore, the demultiplexing of mixed polarity words poses a significant challenge that is not addressed by these models. The findings of this research highlight the limitations of word embedding models in this context and provide a foundation for further improvement. The evaluation framework developed here can be applied to other corpora and other word embedding models, offering a standardized metric for evaluating the quality of these models. The study also yields insights into the complex relationships between words and their context, which can be leveraged to guide future work in natural language processing. This article presents SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems that yield the same overall performance as the optimal wideband waveforming network described in [1]. We show that both these systems are equivalent in terms of their achievable rates to the baseline WBB-SC-OFDM system from [1]. Furthermore, they boast the same non-triviality properties as their SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM counterparts from [1]. Consequently, any results established in [1] are directly applicable to these systems. Moreover, we provide a new intuitive reason for the effectiveness of wideband waveforming, stemming from the notion of effective antenna gain. This effective antenna gain gain can be particularly useful in treating SISO and MISO scenarios. For the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems, we also establish the non-triviality property, thereby ensuring their inclusion in the set of systems considered in [1]. This further incorporation enables us to utilize the results from [1] to derive new important findings, including a key integer programming challenge. Lastly, we offer a concrete example of a real-world system that can be analyzed using the SISO-OFDM framework. This example is pertinent to a specific joint data and power transfer scenario. In this context, the effective antenna gain gain proves particularly advantageous, as it yields a key performance metric. On the other hand, the integer programming challenge does not offer any additional useful information. In contrast, it yields a meaningless result for the same joint data and power transfer scenario when the same SISO-OFDM system is used. This system is now referred to as the "twisted" SISO-OFDM system. This finding is quite interesting as it demonstrates how a seemingly minor change can result in a situation where the integer programming challenge no longer provides any useful information about the performance of the system. This is because the transition from the regular SISO-OFDM system to the twisted SISO-OFDM system is analogous to changing the number of antennas from an odd number to an even number, which in turn is analogous to changing the number of antennas from $n$ to $n-1$, as long as $n$ is an odd number. This situation is further analyzed in the paper, as it results in another integer programming challenge that provides a valid performance metric for the same joint data and power transfer scenario. In multiagent competitions, considering only rational players whose actions are based on truthful comparisons can lead to misinterpretations of the obtained equilibria. This issue arises because, without knowing the relative preferences between all players, it's impossible to determine the pure strategy profile that is rationalizable by all of them. This paper presents an efficient algorithm for identifying a set of actions that could be part of a Nash equilibrium, given observations of players' past actions and their individual binary comparison matrices. This solution works for any number of players and provides the unique rationalizable equilibrium when the number of players is known to be two. Furthermore, our approach facilitates methods for learning the rationalizable equilibrium through reinforcement learning. To demonstrate the practical usefulness of our approach, we showed that it can be applied to two-player multi-armed bandit problems. This led to a rationalizable policy that consistently outperformed several baselines in simulated experiments. This finding was observed across various scenarios, including contexts with changing payoff matrices. This research was preceeded by a conference publication at the 2020 AAAI. An analysis of a stochastic SIR model with temporary removal of susceptible individuals from a network is conducted to examine its applicability to real-world scenarios. The model in question assumes that susceptible individuals are removed from the network at a rate proportional to their connections, and it features a distribution of short-term connections that follow a power law. The model's properties are then compared to a related model with a fixed average connection duration. It is discovered that the model with temporary removals exhibits an accelerated phase early on, where the rate of infection decline outpaces the rate at which new infections occur. However, this accelerated phase is followed by a slowed-down phase, where the rate of infection decline slows down and eventually approaches the same rate as the rate of new infections. This result is further illustrated through numerical examples. A critical finding of this study is that the model with temporary removals exhibits two distinct pandemic phases, separated by a critical point where the distribution of short-term connections exhibits a power law behavior. Ultimately, the analysis of the model with temporary removals provides valuable insights into the dynamics of epidemics, which can be utilized for developing more effective public health strategies. The model in question can also be applied to the analysis of other propagation phenomena in complex networks, including the spread of fires, rumors, and information. The study of a simple metapopulation model with a power law distribution of component sizes is another significant finding of this research, which can be applied to the analysis of other propagation phenomena in complex networks, including the spread of fires, rumors, and information. The study of a simple metapopulation model with a power law distribution of component sizes is another significant finding of this research, which discovers that the coexistence of a main population and a minority population can occur when the minority population occupies a network with a narrow interface, indicating that there are areas where the distribution of component sizes exhibits a power law behavior and thus providing a new possible explanation for this phenomenon. The research also explores three real-world examples, including the spread of an infection in a remote indigenous community, the spread of an infection in a network of villages, and the spread of an forest fire in a network of clear-cuts, which all exhibit a power law distribution of component sizes. Integrating PDF fitting with theoretical frameworks, especially those that incorporate multiple processes and corrections, is a complex task. For the PDF fitting community, accessing accurate, experimentally verified predictions relies on incorporating these comprehensive frameworks into PDF fitting tools. A proposed theory framework, built using the Drell-Yan process as a test case, aims to provide an adaptable structure for researchers to easily incorporate new processes and inputs. This framework is compatible with widely used PDF fitting tools like APFEL, QCDNUM, and VPDF, and incorporates processes in a way that allows for multiple processes to be treated as sources of systematic uncertainty. Verifying the framework's validity, process-by-process analysis has shown that it accurately replicates the underlying dynamics, and this theory framework is available for other processes and other processes' inputs. Further development of this framework is needed to make it a fully autonomous PDF fitting tool. Until then, it can be accessed in its current form at github.com/theory-group-0/TheoryPDF.

To improve policy optimization, Variance Reduction by Experience Replay (VRED2) selectively applies reinforcement learning reinforcement to enhance the current policy, prioritizing the maximum variance observed in recorded exploration data. This results in a more adaptive and efficient approach than conventional policy optimization methods. Our experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that VRED2 leads to enhanced policy performance, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, VRED2 exhibits versatility, compatible with a range of policy-based learning methods. Our analysis highlights the variance-driven nature of VRED2, illustrating its connection to the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Furthermore, we present a more robust variant of VRED2, VRED2+, which incorporates a value-function-based bias correction, thereby addressing the challenge of large value-function gaps. Our findings with VRED2+, evaluated across more complex domains, reveal its ability to handle larger value-function gaps and domain-scale tasks. Our risk-aware VRED2 variant, Risk-Aware VRED2, prioritizes safe policy optimization, whereas our VRED2-SARSA variant, VRED2-SARSA, presents a straightforward way to combine VRED2 with value-function-based methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulam-saqib/vedeep-rl.

This solver has been applied to a range of conformally coupled gravity variants, which exhibit unique and contrasting behavior in our laboratory-scale simulations. However, such models may have value in altered gravity scenarios, mimicking the effects of mass loss or redistribution, and could be readily integrated into existing N-body simulation tools. This research investigates an intricate problem involving acoustic forcing of a turbulent jet flame in an enclosed space. When a jet flame burns within an enclosed environment, it can be subject to oscillations that may cause the flame to become disordered, potentially leading to harmful effects such as explosion-induced building collapse. Consequently, controlling these oscillations and maintaining a stable flame are critical concerns. An active flame method is proposed, where a pilot flame is used to ignite the main fuel stream, offering greater flexibility, including the capacity to introduce acoustic forcing that can influence the stability of the flame. This active flame configuration allows for a direct connection between the fuel and air streams, eliminating the need for a separate acoustic chamber. As a result, the problem of jet flame combustion can be represented by a set of complex equations involving interactions between massless particles, turbulent jets, and acoustic streams. A linearized formulation is then employed to analyze the stability of the flame, resulting in a non-linear equation that requires solving for each cross-section of the jet. A novel feature of this research involves demonstrating the applicability of the linearized framework to specific scenarios of acoustic forcing, including situations where the flame exhibits helical instability. Furthermore, this approach enables the derivation of precise expressions that define the oscillation frequencies of the jet flame, as well as the conditions necessary for its stability. A comprehensive set of equations has been developed that can be applied to a variety of closed environments, ranging from infinitely long pipes to enclosed spaces with reflecting walls, allowing for the direct computation of stream velocities, flame lengths, and the distribution of massless particles along the jet. A special case of this model is then compared to an existing model presented by Trouvé and Vivenie, demonstrating its superiority. This research has been published in the journal Combustion and Flame, available online. A related study involving the application of this method to a more complex scenario of acoustic forcing, including the helical instability of the jet flame, has also been published in the journal Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, available online. A numerical simulation of a jet flame with acoustic forcing has been compared to this linearized model, demonstrating both the accuracy of the model and the complexity of the simulation. A discussion has been presented on the different possible approaches to the linearization of this model, as well as the issues related to the acoustic forcing of a open-ended jet, including the difficulty of predicting the frequency of the oscillations, of the length of the flame, and of the distribution of the massless particles along the jet. Recently, the human genome was thoroughly examined through the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) project, yielding a vast amount of data on active genetic elements, their locations, and interactions. While proponents of the project claim it marks a significant milestone in understanding human biology, some remain skeptical about its practical applications, particularly in pinpointing genetic causes of specific diseases. To address these concerns and evaluate the project's utility, we examined 18 distinct traits or conditions, incorporating data from the 1000 Genomes Project, GWAS studies, and ENCODE. By correlating GWAS associations with active genetic elements, as well as their regulatory relationships, we found a notable number of connections, many of which had been overlooked in existing GWAS studies. Furthermore, we identified potential paths through which genetic variations could influence gene expression, although these were less frequent. Our analysis suggests that a large portion of the genome remains unexamined, particularly in the ENCODE project's focus on actively transcribed regions. Considering that about 70% of the genome is composed of noncoding DNA, a more comprehensive analysis is necessary to uncover dormant or tissue-specific genetic elements. On the other hand, our study also highlights the project's value in providing a rich source of data that can be used to understand the biological mechanisms underlying specific diseases, although more work is needed to fully utilize this information effectively. On a related note, a similar analysis was conducted using data from the Mouse Genome Institute, yielding similar results, although with some notable differences, particularly with regard to genome-wide associations for certain traits that are unique to mice. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring patterns of behavior. This study contradicts this idea by revealing that many neutron star binary systems with low masses do not exhibit regular patterns of behavior, but rather exhibit long periods of activity separation that defy prediction, and that there is no statistical difference between the distribution of recurring and non-recurring patterns of behavior. Consequently, the notion that these sources are necessarily black holes does not seem certain, and alternative explanations for their behavior should also be considered. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the concept of activity separation can be clouded by incomplete data sets, which may result from the limited observational record of these sources, and that activity separation cannot be reliably determined without comprehensive observations of these sources over a substantial duration. Lastly, we highlight the possibility that the majority of the known neutron star binary systems with low masses could actually be misclassified as black hole candidates within the Milky Way and other galaxies.

THz spinning of magnetic nanoparticles has shown vast potential for tackling various applications, but its practical use is limited due to insufficient understanding of the particle's internal mechanics, specifically the dynamic interactions between electrons, vibrations, and spins. In this research, we focus on inertial mechanics and its impact on the spin-vibration interaction. By accounting for inertial effects, we've developed a theoretical framework that incorporates both electron-phonon and spin-vibration interactions. This framework provides a precise description of angular momentum dissipation and its influence on the spreading of spin and vibration. Additionally, it enables tracking of angular momentum components, which are crucial for correctly interpreting time-domain signals. As a concrete example, we apply this developed framework to simulate the spinning of a monolayer graphene flake. High-speed spinning leads to a phenomenon known as "phonon-squeezing," where the angular momentum is rapidly distributed across different phonon modes. Conversely, in a stationary state, the phonon distribution returns to its initial unsqueezed form. This theoretical understanding and our "phonon-squeezing" finding can be experimentally verified using state-of-the-art techniques such as graphene grown on silicon carbide. This growth method allows for direct observation of phonon populations via photoluminescence spectra. This approach can also be extended to other 2D materials grown on various substrates. This research highlights the significance of considering inertial mechanics in the study of spin-vibration interaction and vibration dynamics in confined environments. It also paves the way for exploring the intricate relationships between electron, vibration, and spin interactions in both theoretical and experimental contexts. This includes studying the spin-vibration interaction in stationary and rotating conditions, investigating the phenomenon of "phonon-squeezing" and its associated mechanical and electromagnetic emissions, and investigating the electron-vibration interaction in stationary conditions. This interaction leads to the formation of mechanical sidebands in the electromagnetic spectra and emulates Josephson-like oscillations between different vibration modes. This finding opens up possibilities for investigating analogous phenomena in other systems, such as rotating and stationary superconducting qubits, as well as investigating the analogs of "phonon-squeezing" and Josephson-like oscillations in these systems. This includes investigating the distribution of quantum entropy across the system, the distribution of angular momentum components, the electromagnetic spectra, and the electromagnetic sidebands, as well as the interaction between the system and its environment, and the system's dimensionality. In conversations, interlocutors typically possess distinct levels of knowledge regarding the topics they are discussing. For example, when inquiring about a movie title, one participant might know the exact name, while the other only knows the plot. We propose the variety of semantic knowledge in a conversation should be measured by the difference between the speakers' natural language inference tasks. To investigate this concept, we present a new task, Natural Language Inference Variety in Conversation (NLI-VC), where two agents with unequal knowledge engage in a conversation, and their language inference relationships are assessed. Unlike existing natural language generation evaluation methods, the degree of variety is objective, reflected directly in the inferred distances between the conversation turns. We outline a straightforward approach to create and evaluate the NLI-VC task, demonstrating varied semantic knowledge in conversation is both necessary and NLU-expert-indifferent. Massive rotating stars face hydrodynamic instability near their equators, which can lead to substantial oblateness. Despite this instability, even denser stars can maintain their mass through gravitational interaction with companion stars in binary systems. To explore the dynamics of these dense stars, we developed a numerical model that accounts for rotation, mass conservation, and hydrodynamic stability. Using this model, we investigated the equilibrium configurations of rotating low-mass stars in binary systems. As expected, the inner edge of their Roche lobe is determined by their conservative tidal interaction with the companion. However, due to their rapid rotation, the edge appears deformed, reaching the mass-shedding limit more slowly. Based on observations suggesting that extremely low-mass stars in binaries can survive mass transfer, we compared our predictions with existing data, finding that dense stars with nearly uniform rotation often occupy the inner regions of their Roche lobes. Furthermore, such stars may exist in short-period binaries with massive white dwarf companions, and could also have highly asymmetric shapes, influenced by their close proximity to their companions and rapid rotation. A well-studied model in this context is the Cayley tree, represented as an undirected graph with a central node connected to many peripheral nodes. Previous research on immunizing a Cayley tree has focused on random attacks, but real-world threats often follow targeted patterns. This study aims to explore the dynamics of a targeted attack on a Cayley tree network. By applying the Bethe tree approximation, we can scale up the analysis to very large networks. Our in-depth examination of a targeted attack yields two key results: firstly, at a network level, the distribution of removed nodes can be approximated by a Poisson distribution; secondly, at a component level, the distribution of an isolated component's size is directly obtainable, even in an dynamic setting. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the distribution of a component's size and the distribution of a random node. This enables us to leverage established theories, such as the Bethe tree's independent node property, to gain a deeper understanding of network dynamics. This study's findings on the distribution of a network's components can be applied to a wide range of phenomena, including the spread of diseases and the protection of networks against targeted attacks. The detection of gravitational waves with sensitivity in the high-frequency range is crucial for analyzing events involving compact binaries and supernovae. However, the ability of interferometric detectors to achieve this range is limited by a phenomenon known as laser light retro-reflection, which causes an unstable effect on the signal. Furthermore, this design offers greater flexibility in allowing for non-zero arm misalignment, provides a clearer indication of the orientation of the gravitational wave signals, and offers a novel approach to extracting information from laser light lost in the detector. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on predicting dual 3D face meshes to account for head orientations and aligning them in a self-consistent manner. By simplifying the problem in this way, we demonstrate that modeling head orientations and face alignment can be handled through separate yet interconnected components. In addition, our approach incorporates an auto-encoder with two latent variables to enable robust reconstruction and address the issue of missing facial data. We have implemented this concept as an end-to-end network called SADRNet and have tested it extensively on the widely-used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets, along with a previously unused but readily available dataset called AFW3D. Our findings, reflected in the resulting 3D face reconstruction and alignment visualizations, demonstrate substantial performance enhancements over existing reference methods. Moreover, we have implemented a simple yet effective occlusion-aware missing data estimation technique called Copy-Paste, which has utility beyond the face reconstruction context. In an inflationary model, a specific range of scalar perturbations can result in the formation of primordial black holes, depending on initial conditions. For most models, this connection is directly linked to the Hubble radius during inflation. However, in certain scenarios, a wider range of perturbations may contribute to black hole formation, as it becomes possible for fluctuations to miss re-entering the Hubble radius before the end of inflation. We examine an inflationary model based on $\alpha$-attractor theory, where we find that a specific resonance of scalar perturbations can cause the disruption of oscillatory modes, leading to an extended post-inflationary period and an increased chance of black hole formation. By accounting for both linear and nonlinear effects on the density fluctuations, we determine the minimum amplitude required for a given scalar perturbation to result in black holes. This threshold is found to be influenced by the specific resonance and can be both nonlinear and dependent on the initial condition. Consequently, we overlie the region of parameter space that leads to black hole formation on a map of scalar perturbations, providing a visual representation of how non-linearly perturbed fluctuations behave in this model. Furthermore, we compare our results to observational limits placed on the density of black holes in the early universe, demonstrating that there is a window of accessibility for this model. Lastly, we discuss the potential for this model to explain certain cosmological phenomena, such as the observed 21cm intensity fluctuations. Additionally, we examine the possibility of modifying the $\alpha$-attractor inflationary theory, presenting a new analytical solution for a related model. This new solution is verified through numerical integration and has distinct features, including the formation of a mini-spacetime and a specific resonance, which can result in black hole formation even at a very small amplitude. It builds on the found in "Rethinking Appropriate PD for ADAS" and "Dense Discriminative Learning" by introducing a new formulation that considers the relationship between a pre-trained network's base model and its fine-tuned version. It leads to a regularizer that ensures the network's ability to generalize, which can be efficiently computed. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), base stations can adjust their transmission schedules independently, yet independently chosen schedules can cause backhaul interference, hindering optimal performance. Lastly, various applications of our framework are exhibited, including evaluation of artificial neural networks, validation of the learning experience, and analysis of Dynamic TDD in a pseudo- Dynamic scenario. Our research facilitates efficient, efficient implementation of Dynamic TDD scheduling, thereby paving the way for widespread adoption in 5G networks. The code for this study is available online at https://github.com/author-name/DTDD-NTD.

Machine learning models, especially those for Natural Language Processing (NLP), are highly sensitive to changes in data, which can lead to significant variations in model performance. This issue is particularly pronounced in situations where small changes in data result in substantial changes in model efficacy. While model selection strategies, such as the "K-fold" method, are commonly employed to evaluate models, they are known to produce unstable results due to the way they divide and combine data. To address this challenge, we propose an alternative validation approach, the "J-K fold" method, designed to minimize the variance of model performance and F1-score calculations. In a case study involving a well-known NLP task, we found that the proposed J-K fold method yielded significantly lower performance variance compared to the standard K-fold method. The fabric of a topological space is an abstract model consisting of points represented as locally defined, smoothly connected surfaces, attached to the space via homeomorphisms. For a simply connected space with a well-defined boundary, its fabric can be visualized as a collection of 2-d disks in a 3-d space. We demonstrate that the fabric of such a space is equivalent to a specific type of simplicial complex, which we call a polyhedron. Next, we show that the space's fabric is hereditarily indecomposable if, and only if, its simplicial subdivision is a clique, a particular type of fully connected subgraph. Finally, we explore the relationship between a space's and its simplicial subdivision's (locally) indecomposable properties. Along the way, we develop techniques for analyzing spaces through their simplicial representations. In the process, we introduce a new topological invariant - the space's polyhedral structure - providing a precise, geometric characterization of a space's topological features. The approach presented here offers a novel, point-free, geometric perspective on the concept of a space, offering opportunities for applying ideas from discrete geometry and graph theory in topological analyses. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, particularly focusing on triangular flow $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. By conducting systematic studies and comparing different model implementations, we found that the indicated anisotropic geometry from participant eccentricity alone is insufficient to accurately predict $v_3$, especially in smaller systems like Cu+Cu collisions. However, when accounting for initial eccentricity across a wide range of $k$ (elliptical component of anisotropic geometry) or using three-particle cumulant measurements to reduce initial geometry effects, we obtained excellent agreement with our transport model's predictions. Additionally, our research demonstrated a linear relationship between the anisotropic flow of charge particles and initial geometry in Au+Au collisions, which was observable across various centralities. Furthermore, by incorporating recombination and fragmentation aspects of our transport model, we were able to explore anisotropic flow's origin and found that it exhibits a similar central charge-dependent pattern in both systems. Our study also highlighted the influence of the string melting assumption in our transport model, which showed that $v_3/\epsilon_3$ is approximately constant across different systems and centralities, and identified potential connections between $v_3$ and medium temperature in Au+Au collisions. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing strategies and proposing innovative ones. Although such methods are invaluable, they share a common limitation: they generally require a very small time step, rendering them impractical for real-world applications involving large time scales. In contrast, iterative solution methods for large systems of equations, which arise from spatial and temporal discretizations of partial differential equations, offer a different set of challenges. While these methods are an essential part of any numerical simulation, altering the original equation's properties is not their primary concern. In fact, many standard techniques can sometimes even disrupt the equation's preserving properties. This study focuses on investigating the impact of these methods on preserving the original equation's properties, with a specific emphasis on linear iterative techniques. A notable discovery of this research involves demonstrating that the linear multistep method's preserving properties are conserved when using appropriate iterative techniques, such as Krylov methods with effective preconditioners. Furthermore, this study provides specific examples of using Krylov methods, including the conjugate gradient and flexible preconditioned GMRES, in solving systems derived from spatial and temporal discretizations of partial differential equations. Soft tissue implants like implants for facial and breast reconstruction require precise volume-to-surface alignment to ensure a natural appearance and function. Traditionally, surgeons rely on their experience to position the implant, but this method has a significant margin of error. To address this challenge, we developed a biomechanical model that aligns soft tissue volumes with a corresponding surface model, based on finite elasticity theory. To train the model and account for varying tissue properties, we used 4D MRI data from 10 subjects. Once trained, the model can align new volume and surface data from a single 3D MRI scan. To evaluate the model, we used 3D prints of the aligned models made from MRI data and photographs of the corresponding areas on real subjects. The results show that the model accurately replicates the natural anatomy of the subjects, with an average error of 4.5 mm when compared to 3D prints and 2 mm when compared to photographs. To further tailor the model to individual needs, we propose using 3D prints of the desired surface, in addition to 4D MRI data, to create a fully customized alignment tool for surgeons. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories of objects within a given point cloud or image. Unlike two-dimensional trajectory estimation, flow estimation must account for both spatial coordinates and velocity components along the x, y, and z axes. To tackle this challenge, researchers have traditionally employed stereo matching in conjunction with optical flow algorithms. Nevertheless, such methods are prone to degradation in low-texture, semi-occluded, and far-away regions with respect to feature extraction and neighbor-based aggregation techniques used in optical flow and stereo matching. To address this limitation, we propose a novel method called Self-Guided Scene Flow Estimation (SGSFE), which leverages a unique adversarial metric learning technique allowing the network to autonomously determine the most reliable points for calculating the motion trajectory. By circumventing neighbor-based aggregation, our method prioritizes points based on their intrinsic similarity to the predicted flow, thereby enhancing accuracy in regions prone to feature extraction difficulties. We also introduce a novel patch-based occlusion detection mechanism and a data-driven loss function that differentiates between point clouds and image-based flow estimation. SGSFE demonstrates superior performance across various point cloud and image-based datasets compared to the current state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, we show that optimizing the network for image-based flow estimation enhances the results obtainable from 3D stereo flow estimation. To replicate our results, we are providing two new datasets: a publicly available point cloud dataset named Middlebury 3DFlow and a private dataset named Stanford 2-23D. Our code is available at https://github.com/yousef-tools/Self-Guided-Scene-Flow-Estimation.

By utilizing a mean-field approximation and a Lagrangian approach from the linear sigma model, we determined the spin-aligned quark matter's thermodynamic properties. This study's outcomes are now available to the scientific community for further analysis and use.

Modern microservices applications comprise diverse, independently developed services that interact via function calls. As a result, these applications are vulnerable to performance issues and security breaches resulting from excessive system call exposure. Existing solutions, such as Google's gVisor, provide a layered isolation framework that enables services to run in a secure environment while making all system calls accessible to all services. However, this approach can lead to call overhead, security conflicts, and an unwieldy permissions matrix. In addition, determining the optimal system call policies for isolated services is a time-consuming and manual process. In this paper, we present Timeloops, a pioneering approach in automatic system call policy learning for containerized microservices. The Timeloops approach learns the system call policies for isolated services through observation of their execution within a gVisor environment. It develops a set of predefined rules based on normal system calls and flags system calls that are considered malicious. In addition, it creates a graphical representation of the services' call relationships and uses it to guide further investigation into any security breaches. We tested Timeloops on real-world applications, including Apache Kafka and Apache EMBEMLD, and our results show that it reduces call overhead, eliminates unnecessary system call exposure, and successfully learns the system call policies for these services. In fact, when tested against benchmarking tools, it demonstrated a performance improvement of ten to a hundred times. Furthermore, it discovered a security breach in one of the tested applications, YSOFT, which it rectified by limiting system call policies. In summary, Timeloops offers an innovative solution to the problems of system call policies in containerized microservices, which includes performance issues, security conflicts, and call exposure. It provides a free download of its source code. In addition, it presented the results of its research at ACM SIGSAC 2022 conference held in Rimini, Italy. In conclusion, Timeloops represents a groundbreaking achievement in autonomous system call policy learning for secure and high-performance system call interactions in containerized microservices applications. In further development, we are enhancing its capabilities to learn policies for services that use shared libraries and to investigate other isolation frameworks. In addition, we are exploring other applications of Timeloops, including its use in learning policies for virtual machines and in discovering security breaches in complex software systems. In addition, we are open to collaborating with interested researchers and developing Timeloops further. In soccer, key moments can greatly impact the outcome of a match.  Team tactics often focus on regaining possession, yet regaining the lead or tying the game in certain situations may yield a more substantial advantage.  Currently, research on soccer tactics is limited, and available data is primarily restricted to passing patterns and score results.  Our work utilizes a publicly available dataset that encompasses passing plots, player positions, and game events, which we combine with a deep reinforcement learning approach to train a strategic decision-making model.  This model enables teams to make informed decisions about player movements and the ball in critical scenarios.  We validate our approach against a purely random decision-making process and observe a significant difference in favorable outcomes.  Specifically, in high-stakes situations, our model yields $21.4\%$ more favorable game situations, as indicated by passing plots, and $13.3\%$ higher chances of scoring, along with a $10.3\%$ lower likelihood of conceding a goal.  Furthermore, we analyze the precursor actions that lead to preferred outcomes and demonstrate how this information can be utilized to create more effective team formations. Seismic waveform inversion aims to create high-quality subsurface models by matching synthetic wavefields with recorded seismic data. However, the problem is known to be computationally intensive and challenging to solve, especially when incorporating complex geological structures. A significant amount of research has focused on accelerating the solver using targeted finite difference methods and advanced optimization techniques. In this study, we explore the use of a time-domain wave equation full waveform inversion method and the conjugate gradient method with a targeted finite difference wave equation solver. When the solver and the wave equation for the forward problem have the same discretization, the conjugate gradient method can be employed to accelerate the solver, and we have tested this approach on synthetic data. Additionally, we have applied this method to real data, specifically the Marmous-24 data set, and have obtained comparable results with the currently available methods. To further improve the convergence rate, we propose a number of strategies, including the use of a more effective initial model, the application of sparse reciprocity data, and the development of a nonlinear conjugate gradient method. These approaches have been successful in reducing the number of iterations required to achieve a given misfit threshold. However, there are still some challenges to be addressed, such as the issue of nonuniqueness in the solution, which needs to be resolved in order to achieve reliable results in real-world applications. In dynamically evolving ecosystems, species can move and compete for space and resources. These interactions lead to a variety of outcomes, including the coexistence of multiple species, the dominance of a single species, or the extinction of one or more species. By analyzing a random field Ising model with time-dependent dynamics, we gained a deeper understanding of how species interaction affects the dynamics and leads to species coexistence, as well as exploring how a tradeoff between competitive ability and colonizing capacity influences the outcome of these interactions. Our findings show that a specific interaction pattern, characterized by the existence of a unique globally accessible state, is necessary for the coexistence of multiple species. Conversely, we found that the elimination of one species is inevitable in a dynamic ecosystem, provided that it is not a dominant state, as it will eventually give way to a dynamic succession where a different species thrives. Our research was further expanded to examine the scenario of multiple species interactions, resulting in the exclusion of all but two species that coexist with each other. The complex dynamics of this model are reflected in a simple mean-field model, which in turn displays a rich dynamics, including the emergence of oscillations, the breaking of symmetry, as well as the two-species coexistence state. The time-dependent dynamics of this model can be very sensitive, leading to the formation of macroscopic coexistence, species elimination, or the formation of domain walls that move over time. Notably, we found that the time-dependent dynamics of the mean-field model can abruptly change its behavior, resulting in the emergence of chaos, which in turn affects the time it takes for the model to switch between different states. Our analysis of the model parameters allows us to identify the conditions under which the model exhibits a uniform state, the formation of domain walls, or the oscillation between different states. Our research provides a dynamic version of the Kuramoto-Sakaguchi model, which displays chaotic behavior, accompanied by competition between two species, resulting in the formation of the macroscopic coexistence state. Our findings show that the time-dependent dynamics of this model is extremely sensitive, leading to the sudden change of its behavior, as well as its ability to switch between different states, including the formation of the macroscopic coexistence state, the elimination of one species, or the formation of the grand canyon state, where a domain wall moves over time. Our analysis of the model parameters allows us to identify the conditions under the model exhibits the macroscopic coexistence state, the grand canyon state, or the oscillation between different states.

By deliberately introducing a quadratic phase error in the electron beam, it can be restored to its original form upon interaction with a specimen, potentially facilitating the correction of aberrations in the TEM. This study investigates the feasibility of employing a programmable phase disc to correct for a range of aberrations, focusing on defocus and astigmatic errors. A preceding study demonstrated the capability of a phase disc to correct defocus. The theory of superradiance suggests that rotating black holes or compact objects should surround themselves with a system of continuously formed, specific-frequency ultralight bosons. Ultra-light bosons such as axions or scalar particles can be identified through observations of quasars, which are powered by supermassive black holes at the center of galaxies. To this end, we examine the spin characteristics of these black holes using the principle of superradiance, which results in the formation of ultralight boson systems at specific frequencies. By linking the system frequencies to the spins and masses of black holes, we can determine the spins of these black holes. Based on a statistical analysis of quasars with known characteristics, including luminosity, redshift, and radio and optical spectral characteristics, our findings suggest that the spins of supermassive black holes are consistently lower than expected, specifically 0.43, which is in line with predictions made by the $\Lambda$CDM model. Furthermore, we find that the distribution of spin characteristics can be explained by a simple model involving a gradual buildup over time, and that the accretion of matter with high spins, as seen in bulge-less galaxies, plays a significant role in this process. Our study highlights the importance of quasars in providing access to black hole spins, and the resulting constraints on ultralight boson masses, which in turn provide insights into the mechanisms of symmetry breaking and the values of GUT-scale parameters. Our analysis also offers a solution to the longstanding problem of spin slowdown, and highlights the predictive power of superradiance in the study of quasars and ultralight bosons. Lastly, our findings in this study offer potential applications in the search for ultralight bosons, which could be modified to target specific frequencies associated with particular quasars or radio pulses, such as those associated with Fast Radio Bursts. The paper addresses the problem of bias in magnetricogram inversion tools, specifically concerning the estimation of solar vector magnetic field data. Recent advancements in data collection have made it possible to accurately determine the orientation of magnetic fields, which is critical for understanding various solar phenomena. However, restricting our knowledge to a narrow range of field inclinations, typically less than 80 degrees, might lead to misconstruing existing data. We examined a substantial dataset comprising approximately 13,000 vector magnetograms from the Solar Optical Observatory and found that the majority can be accurately analyzed using existing inversion tools with a precision of about 5 degrees. We also discovered biases in two widely used inversion methods, particularly with LANL-IDT and PHIS, especially for magnetograms featuring strong field inclinations greater than 45 degrees. To address these issues, we propose adjusting the analysis conditions for these inversion methods and provide tailored profiles to alleviate the observed biases. Finally, we highlight the importance of thorough validation in the development of inversion algorithms and stress the need for more precise modeling of magnetic field orientations. Understanding and rectifying these biases is crucial for analyzing current and future solar data, which can be analyzed using the recently developed Solar Vector Magnetometer Inversion Assessment Tool. Moreover, correcting these biases is necessary for correctly applying the Milne-Eddington inversion method, which is a fundamental aspect of analyzing spectrographic data, such as the Solar Dynamics Observatory's interface with the AIA/SDO. The updated conditions and profiles we provided can be applied to other datasets, including those obtained from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, which has been collecting data since 2010. The paper's findings and recommendations aim to improve the precision of vector magnetogram estimation, which is a critical step for analyzing various solar phenomena and studying magnetic field dynamics on the sun. In a world where training data for a specific task is scarce, being able to leverage related tasks with abundant data would greatly benefit model performance. However, this assumes that the related tasks can be easily identified, which is not always the feasible outcome of many real-world applications. We introduce a novel approach called Retrieval-Augmented Data Augmentation (RDA), a method that combines two techniques: unsupervised cross-task representation learning and data augmentation via retrieval. RDA employs the non-parametric cross-task representation learning to obtain a task-agnostic embedding space where similar tasks are represented by similar embeddings. In this space, we utilize a query-by-example approach to gather a pool of instance embeddings that represent instances from the target task, which are then used to generate novel training examples. We evaluate RDA on multiple datasets and find that it consistently boosts performance in low-data regimes. Moreover, RDA demonstrates adaptability and versatility, as it can be integrated into existing models with the addition of a single module. The code for RDA is publicly available at: https://github.com/ghruvo/rda. Additionally, we present an interactive visualization of the results on the Wiki Fonts task. UCDA employs a nearest neighbor search to generate new training instances from a related task. Moreover, UCDA demonstrates adaptability and versatility, as it can be integrated into existing models with the addition of a single module. Implementing differential privacy in the context of deep learning models involves several challenges, primarily due to the need for a consistent application of privacy-preserving mechanisms across various hyperparameters for optimization algorithms. Traditional methods for achieving differential privacy focus primarily on modifying algorithms to limit information disclosure. In contrast, most current approaches in DPML research rely on theoretical frameworks without consideration for the impact of hyperparameters. This paper focuses on the practical issue of tuning hyperparameters for the stochastic gradient descent algorithm in deep learning, including the selection of batch sizes and optimization algorithms. However, we have found that conventional approaches to hyperparameter tuning can lead to the accidental disclosure of sensitive information, as they result in the preferential use of certain batch sizes and algorithms based on data characteristics. To address this issue, we propose a novel method called DPHyper, a general framework for hyperparameter tuning in DPML that incorporates a new form of batch size modification and a system of rules for algorithm selection. This framework provides a means of converting algorithm-dependent tasks into tasks that depend only on the data, thus ensuring that the information disclosed is limited to what is contained in the data itself. This is demonstrated through a set of experiments conducted using both widely-used and less common datasets. The results show that DPHyper leads to a more uniform distribution of hyperparameters, reduces the risk of biased algorithm selection, and results in differentiable privacy costs, all of which result in a more robust and less biased deployment of deep learning models with a given level of differential privacy. This is achieved through the application of robust baselines, such as distributed SGD and federated learning, as well as adaptive approaches, including transfer learning, meta-learning, and batch size tuning, which provide meaningful improvements over conventional approaches. This research offers a novel perspective on hyperparameter tuning in DPML, which can be used as a starting point for further exploration into the challenges of model selection and feature engineering. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. We present a novel approach to interpreting network behavior by applying the neural network tool, known as a network interpreter. Our analysis of a sample network using the interpreter reveals the meaning of each loss function component, allowing us to identify the underlying network behavior. We further use this approach to investigate network behavior in a real-world dataset, discovering that loss function impact can vary depending on network depth. We also find that the standard loss function may need to be modified depending on dataset characteristics, such as class balance. Our research highlights the importance of selecting an appropriate loss function, given the numerous options available, making it one of the paper's main contributions. We believe this work can serve as a starting point for further research on the complex dynamics of neural network loss functions. Our code is available online at \url{https://github.com/}.

This research involves conducting a computational heat and mass transfer analysis to simulate the crystallization of isotactic poly(1,2-butene) (iPB2). When stretched, iPB2 exhibits unique crystallization characteristics. To accurately replicate these processes, a finite element method was employed and the results compared to available experimental data, showing the model's effectiveness in simulating stretching-induced crystallization, including surface and internal void formation, material density, and temperature changes. The study also explores the impact of mesh density, time steps, and material properties on the simulation outcomes. A notable observation from the analysis involves the formation of surface voids being unaffected by the finite deformation model used, which was initially suspected but required verification through the simulation. The proposed model has been successfully applied to replicate the complex processes occurring during the stretching of iPB2, offering a valuable tool for future processing and material design modifications. The research was conducted in collaboration with colleagues from the Polymers Department at the Institute of Physical Chemistry of the Polish Academy of Sciences in Krakow. The simulation code has been made available online. The material parameters and stretching conditions required for densification, surface void formation, and complete crystallization were determined and varied to simulate different processing conditions. The results show that changing the draw ratio leads to material densification but also causes surface voids to form, while increasing the stretch rate results in surface void formation instead of densification, and varying the initial void fraction affects the material's crystallization behavior. The study demonstrates how the simulation model can be used to analyze the complex relationships between material structure, stretching conditions, and the resulting microstructure, as shown in the equation $\phi_c=\phi_0e^{\frac{2.5\rho_c}{\rho_0}(\lambda-1)}$, where $\phi_c$ represents the final void fraction, $\rho_c$ and $\rho_0$ are the material densities after and before stretching, and $\lambda$ is the draw ratio. The simulation outcomes also highlight the importance of considering material anisotropy when analyzing the stretching-induced anisotropy of iPB2, the effects of temperature on the material's viscosity and crystallization behavior, and the impact of void formation on material anisotropy and crystallization, as demonstrated in the images and equations provided. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. As a result, non-coherent methods have been explored, often showing comparable performance. However, these schemes typically sacrifice further robustness, which is gained by non-differential methods. Non-coherent CPM detection can be made more resilient to delay by employing differential techniques. This paper presents a range of discrete CPM constellations that are resistant to delay-caused symbol confusion. For these constellations, we establish conditions under which differential detection is effective. Additionally, we demonstrate ways to enhance existing ones. Moreover, this paper delves into various baseband CPM detection techniques, including coherent, non-coherent, differential, and non-differential methods. This enables us to focus on delay-tolerant, end-to-end equivalent differential detection protocols. As a key contribution, we establish that delay-tolerant differential detection works optimally when the CPM signal has a specific, uniquely defined constellation that is resistant to rotation. This optimal constellation maximizes the minimum Euclidean distance between confused symbols. This minimum distance is crucial because it directly affects the performance of delay-tolerant differential detection. Furthermore, we provide a critical analysis of various CPM signal configurations, including their equivalents, and demonstrate how delay-tolerant differential detection can be implemented in several scenarios.
