In 1978, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper richness in graphs, introducing a concept that helps identify Ramsey-like properties in infinite graphs. They also established a significant theorem linking the Ramsey upper richness of infinite graph partitions to the Ramsey property of their subgraphs. This article extends that theorem by demonstrating that an infinite graph's Ramsey upper richness is equivalent to the Ramsey property of its largest component. Additionally, we provide a novel characterization of the Ramsey upper richness in infinite graph partitions, which can be applied to exhibit an infinite sequence of distinct infinite graphs exhibiting the Ramsey property. These results build upon the foundational work of Erdos and Galvin, as well as a recent finding by the current author, and encompass a broader class of infinite graphs, including those with components possessing the Ramsey property but not the full Ramsey property. This is achieved through a more nuanced definition of upper richness, which can be applied to infinite graphs containing components with the Ramsey property. This new standard of upper richness is referred to as definable upper richness. This article also explores connections between this new standard of upper richness, other established graph theories, such as Sigma-ramsey theory and its various iterations. Furthermore, we provide a list of open problems related to these theories. These problems pertain to the relationship between the Ramsey upper richness of an infinite graph and its largest component, as well as the connection between the Ramsey upper richness of an infinite graph and the Ramsey property of its subgraphs of finite size. These open problems can be applied to any infinite graph, including those with the Ramsey property or those possessing the Ramsey property at every finite depth. This list also includes problems that can be applied to infinite graphs with the Ramsey property or those possessing the Ramsey property at every finite depth, such as those with the Borel Ramsey property, the weak Ramsey property, or the property of having a Ramsey subtree of a specific height. These open problems relate to these exclusive cases as well. This article is intended for researchers with an advanced background in Ramsey theory, specifically those with a deep understanding of infinite graphs and their associated theories. A novel employment for simulating massless Dirac fermions in (1+1)D space is proposed, leveraging quantum circuits with excess ancilla qubits. Originally, quantum circuit simulations are limited by the inevitability of decoherence from interactions with their environment. By employing qutrits instead of qubits, the rate of this decoherence is significantly reduced, although it inevitably leads to circuit complexity and a resulting time-dependent effect on the simulation results. A strategy is presented to mitigate this impact by adopting a suitable initial state for the ancilla qutrits, one that minimizes the effect of decoherence on key spectral properties of the simulated model. As a specific application, this method is shown to efficiently simulate the dimerized su(2) chain, a well-studied model with both semi-Dirac and gapped phases, by analyzing spectral gaps, spectral widths, and energy spectra obtained from time-evolved simulations. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential of small-scale, noise-sensitive quantum devices in accurately simulating complex systems and provides a framework for effectively utilizing qutrits as ancillas in quantum simulations. The research is further expanded to explore the integration of discrete time-modulated driving protocols that accurately simulate the interaction of fermionic systems with external influences, offering a more realistic and precise simulation of real-world systems. The findings are relevant to a broader context, extending far beyond qutrit-based simulations to covering general principles applicable to noise-induced errors in quantum simulations, including those employing qubits. The research is accompanied by publicly accessible code, available at https://github.com/Quantum-Group/sQED-simulation. The code utilizes the QuTip++ library, a Python framework for solving the time-evolved open quantum systems. The research was conducted without the aid of a supercomputer, demonstrating the feasibility of simulations on mid-range hardware. The results of the simulations are presented in the accompanying figures, which include the calculated spectra obtained from time-evolved simulations, as well as energy spectra obtained via numerical analysis, and are also summarized in the tables provided. A recent survey of far-infrared bright cores in the Dragon infrared dark nebula reveals the presence of massive protostar and star-forming cores. Analyzing these cores with a two-parameter model, we found that most cores can be represented by a mixture of dusty interstellar grains and a foreground screen causing extinction. The massive protostar and star-forming cores are primarily found in the northern sector of the nebula, and are linked by filamental structures that may indicate the path these cores are following as they move towards forming a massive central star or cluster. The distribution of these cores is influenced by both magnetic fields and gravitational forces, and their development is likely unaffected by external influences such as nearby suns. The formation of these cores is likely the precursor to the formation of massive stars in the center of the nebula, and the study of the Dragon nebula provides a unique glimpse at this process. The relationship between these cores and the surrounding magnetic and gravitational forces can be further understood by comparing the Dragon nebula to a model of a collapsing molecular cloud. The study also found that the mass distribution of the cores in the Dragon nebula is similar to the distribution found in the Taurus molecular cloud, but the cores in the Dragon nebula are more concentrated and have a greater mass range. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by a rough surface's texture, which can be hazardous for safe operation in various industries that deal with fluids and surface interactions. Despite the importance of this issue, there is a lack of information on the flow behavior related to different surface textures, particularly for highly non-Newtonian fluids. In this study, we investigate the flow behavior of a foam that flows over various textured surfaces with different geometries, such as squares, circles, and triangles, by analyzing both static and dynamic situations. Our key observation shows that foam flows prefer certain directions that are influenced by the arrangement of air pockets and depend on the texture's pattern. Moreover, our data reveal the different ways textures affect the flow's speed, both with and without the presence of bubbles breaking away from the surface. Our findings also indicate that even a very subtle texture can raise the threshold for flow to occur and slow down the flow's speed, even in dynamic situations. Our research provides a better understanding of how textures affect fluid flow and can be applied to predict safe operating speeds for smooth or textured surfaces used in various industrial applications. Our data and analysis are available to the scientific community.

The number of skin cancers is rising worldwide, due in part to increased awareness and reporting, making accurate diagnosis crucial.  A significant challenge in treating skin cancers is achieving a definitive diagnosis, as many patients present with more than one type of skin lesion, making it difficult to establish a correct differential diagnosis.  To complicate matters further, dermatologists must consider the patient's medical history, skin lesions, and physical characteristics, along with any associated symptoms, which can be expressed in a variable and uncertain manner.  As a result, learning from a single case is extremely challenging, if not impossible.  To address this issue, a machine learning-based approach is proposed, focusing on a technique called outlier detection to identify cancers that are difficult to diagnose.  The proposed method uses five classifiers, which are then analyzed to determine how they classify samples as normal or outlier cancer types.  The proposed approach determines the best combination of classifiers that minimize both classification and reconstruction error.  The proposed technique is evaluated using real data from the Dermatology Institute, which shows that the proposed method achieves a high level of accuracy in identifying cancer types that are difficult to diagnose.  The results highlight the effectiveness of the proposed approach in identifying outlier cancer samples, even in cases where there are few training examples.  The proposed method has the potential to be a valuable tool for dermatologists, enabling them to accurately identify cancers that are difficult to diagnose, even with limited training and patient data.  The proposed approach can be applied to other medical fields, such as identifying difficult-to-diagnose prostate or breast cancer cases. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that traditional attention mechanisms, although effective, can be inefficient, particularly when producing the initial target words, where they often fail to accurately identify relevant source tokens. We propose an innovative look-forward attention mechanism, designed to streamline the attention process by bypassing the encoding step and allowing direct comparison between source and target word embeddings. This approach is particularly beneficial for initializing the attention process, where it leads to a more precise alignment, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of neural machine translation. Experimental evaluations, conducted on vast translation datasets, demonstrate the proposed look-forward attention mechanism's superiority over conventional attention, yielding significant improvements in translation quality. Moreover, the mechanism's efficiency is showcased by its ability to excel in other tasks, including summarization. The code for the proposed model is available at github.com/THU-CLSL/look-forward-attention.

The GCF's innovative features included a type system, routing mechanisms, and customizable services. Over time, the framework's limitations became apparent, particularly in performance and scalability. As a result, the project was rebranded as the CoGKit grid toolkit. Although the original name reflected the team's ambition to create a universal grid computing framework, in vain. Nevertheless, the technological advancements and lessons learned from this project were valuable, and its legacy can be seen in various subsequent applications, including the Australian National Virtual Observatory. The project's difficulties also informed the design of its successors, including the Wellington Architecture, the CoGKit Services Architecture, and the Australian National e-Infrastructure for Data, the ANEDIs. The ANEDIs in turn has influenced the development of the Australian National Virtual Observatory, the Square Kilometre Array software systems, and the European Southern Observatory's Research Data Management Architecture. The story of the GCF highlights the challenges of building a universal grid computing platform and the importance of a nuanced understanding of the problem domain. The project's legacy is a testament to the value of persistent, open-source development and the benefits derived from international collaborations. A study was conducted to understand the plasma produced by the generator's helicon source, with particular focus on verifying its operation in the helicon regime. In recent years, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have gained significant traction in processing complex graph data, with applications in vital areas such as social network analysis and molecular chemistry study. To enhance understanding of fundamental GCNN components, we propose a novel analysis based on signal processing principles. Specifically, we reinterpret convolution operations in GCNNs as a combination of signal filtering techniques. By applying a matched filtering approach, we provide insights into how information is extracted from local neighborhoods during GCNN convolution. Furthermore, a signal representation model is presented to describe node representation updates, revealing that GCNNs using multi-layer convolution are equivalent to a particular signal processing scenario. A numerical study is conducted to compare our analysis method with existing GCNN models, demonstrating consistency and validating our signal processing-based analysis. Lastly, we offer a code implementation of our proposed methodology. High-performance computing resources were used for this project, specifically IBM Research's Darwin Supercomputer, located at Yale University.

In the context of online learning, the $k$-means clustering algorithm groups $k$ objects into clusters based on their feature vectors, with the aim of minimizing the within-cluster variance. However, implementing this algorithm is challenging due to the need for frequent recalculation of cluster centers and identification of significant changes in data. To address this issue, we developed a revised algorithm called Dynamic $k$-means Grouping, which detects and adapts to changes in data by employing a thresholded system similar to ExpGrowth, while guaranteeing nearly optimal performance in terms of variance and cluster centers' distance from their optimal counterparts. Specifically, our results show that the algorithm can maintain clusters that are within a factor of $O(\sqrt{k}\cdot \sigma \cdot t^{1/4})$ from the optimal variance and cluster centers' distance, where $\sigma$ represents the dimension of the feature space and $t$ denotes time. Moreover, cluster centers can be updated in $O(k^{3/2} \cdot \sigma^{3/2} \cdot \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)} \cdot \sqrt{t})$ time, with probabilities of failure less than $\delta$. We have also introduced a variance-clustering tree data structure, which is more efficient in terms of memory usage and allows for faster query processing. Finally, our algorithm's performance has been compared with existing dynamic $k$-means algorithms, demonstrating its superior performance in terms of variance and cluster centers' distance from their optimal counterparts. This has been substantiated through extensive simulations conducted using both synthetic and real-world data. Lastly, we have outlined possible modifications to the algorithm, as well as its potential applications in various contexts. In this research, we explore efficient methods for determining the rapidity of proton beams in high-energy muon collisions. Due to the lack of electromagnetic attachments to the collider, detecting the beam's rapidity is more challenging than measuring its energy. We review existing techniques for determining the electron beam's rapidity at electron-proton colliders and identify two effective approaches: (1) identifying neutral current interactions and calculating the average rapidity of all such events, (2) using leading neutrons from deep inelastic scattering to directly determine the beam's rapidity. We also consider the feasibility of these methods at a future high-energy muon collider, with a focus on optimizing detector design to facilitate efficient beam closure. To facilitate smooth closure, we outline possible detector configurations, including placing detectors at the front and back of the collider, and evaluate the effectiveness of these designs using simulations. In particular, we find that a mid-rapidity detector placement is superior for determining the beam's rapidity, while a forward detector placement is more effective for directly measuring the beam's rapidity via leading neutrons. In addition, we discuss the statistical precision of beam closure achievable in a muon collider compared to an electron-proton collider, and explore the potential of a muon collider for carrying out neutrino oscillation experiments with matter effects. In such a case, we find that a 10 GeV muon collider with a beam current of 50 $\mu$A and 100 $\mu$A would be sufficient to determine the neutrino oscillation parameters with high precision within a year of operation. In the process, we provide comprehensive simulations of one of the possible detector configurations, consisting of a lead-scintillator detector with a length of 5 meters, a width of 1 meter, and a height of 1 meter, placed at a detector acceptance of 80-100 GeV in a muon collider with a beam energy of 100 GeV. These simulations enable the simultaneous measurement of neutrino oscillation parameters and the proton beam's rapidity in a muon collider. In multi-task reinforcement learning, environments from different tasks can vary independently. When tasks are similar, it's essential to avoid interfering information. We introduce a method to break down policies into modular systems, separating independent and interfering information. This approach ensures that each system learns only from information relevant to its associated task. We show that agent performance similar to non-modular systems can be achieved when tasks are similar, and a new way of analyzing multi-task value functions is provided. Additionally, our approach is effective in solving decoy tasks that are misleading and confusing. We also explore how to determine the appropriate level of modularity. Our modular system is applicable to both continuous and discrete action spaces. Our approach is tested on a decoy task and a complex multi-task environment composed of sub-systems, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ghul131/mbrl-mtl-modular-systems.

Recently, machine learning techniques, especially GAN-based methods, have been applied to unresolved signal identification problems in neuroscience. A key concept in classical dynamical systems is the presence of invariant surfaces, which remain unchanged under the system's flow and can be identified by their stationary points. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to synthesize raw audio time series with several key variations, including those found in speech, polyphonic music, and animal sounds. By extending the conventional WaveNet architecture, which is known for its high-quality audio generation but has a significant computational footprint, QPNet introduces a new Convolution Neural Network (CNN) with dynamic dilation periods that are sensitive to the spectral characteristics of the signal. This CNN is used in a transposed WaveNet structure, leveraging the inherent properties of signal periods to accelerate modeling and generation. Experimental evaluations of QPNet on speech, polyphonic music, and animal sounds demonstrate the effectiveness of this model, showing it can produce high-quality audio that is indistinguishable from the original recordings. Code for QPNet is available open-source on GitHub. This work also discusses a simplified version of the model, called Reduced QPNet, which further minimizes the computational requirements while maintaining comparable audio quality. In assessments of reduced QPNet on speech, it outperforms existing models in terms of compression ratio, while on polyphonic music and animal sounds, it shows a significant decrease in quality scores. This suggests that QPNet may have difficulty handling sounds with irregular periods, prompting possible future improvements. In addition, we explore the use of QPNet as an autoregressive encoder, obtaining a perceptual embedding that reflects the spectral analysis of the signal, which can be used to guide sampling in the generative process, resulting in improved sample diversity. This approach can be applied to real-world sounds with complex time-series structures, demonstrating the applicability of this model to such tasks.
